title: "Learn Statistics Through EDI: Experiments with Known Truth"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

## A note for instructors

Most statistical ideas are statements about what happens *over many repetitions*
of an experiment: an estimator is unbiased, a test rejects 5% of the time, an
interval covers the truth 95% of the time. Students usually take these on faith,
because in a real data set the truth is unknown and the experiment happens once.

In a simulation the truth is known, because you plant it. EDI (Experimental Design
and Inference) builds randomized experiments the way they are run in practice:
a design object assigns treatment, you record the responses, and an inference
object estimates the effect. If you generate the responses yourself, with a
treatment effect `beta_T` that you chose, you can run the same experiment a few
hundred times and watch an idea happen.

The eight lessons below are standalone. Each one needs only `library(EDI)`, sets
its own seed, and can be assigned on its own. Each has a short statement of the
idea, code that runs as written, one figure, a takeaway and two or three
exercises. The code uses plain `for` loops rather than a simulation framework so
that every step of the repetition is visible.

Every lesson uses the same four steps:

```{r pattern, eval = FALSE}
des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)  # 1. a design
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)                                            # 2. the subjects
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()                                                   #    and their assignment
w = des$get_w()                                                                  #    (0 = control, 1 = treatment)
des$add_all_subject_responses(y)                                                 # 3. the responses
inf = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)              # 4. an analysis
inf$compute_estimate()
```

Students who do not want to install R can run every lesson in a browser tab: see
[Try EDI in your browser](try-edi-in-your-browser.html). In the browser, divide the
number of repetitions by about four; the figures get noisier but tell the same
story.

Simulation results are themselves estimates. A rejection rate estimated from
`R` repetitions has a Monte Carlo standard error of about
$\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}$, which for $p = 0.05$ and $R = 1000$ is about 0.007. The lessons
quote this error where it matters.

## Lesson 1: Why randomize?

**The idea.** In an observational comparison, whoever chooses the treatment may
choose it for reasons that also affect the outcome. Here older subjects are more
likely to be treated, and age raises the outcome, so the treated group would have
higher outcomes even with no treatment at all. The difference in means then
mixes the treatment effect with the age difference. A randomized design breaks
the link between age and treatment, so the same difference in means is centered
on the truth.

```{r lesson1}
set.seed(101)
n = 100
beta_T = 1                         # the planted treatment effect
R = 500                            # number of repeated experiments

est_biased = numeric(R)
est_random = numeric(R)
for (i in 1:R) {
  age = rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10)
  noise = rnorm(n, sd = 2)

  # (a) a biased rule: the older the subject, the likelier they are treated
  w_biased = rbinom(n, 1, plogis((age - 50) / 5))
  y_biased = beta_T * w_biased + 0.2 * age + noise
  est_biased[i] = mean(y_biased[w_biased == 1]) - mean(y_biased[w_biased == 0])

  # (b) a randomized EDI design: half the subjects treated, chosen at random
  des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(age = age))
  des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  w = des$get_w()
  des$add_all_subject_responses(beta_T * w + 0.2 * age + noise)
  inf = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
  est_random[i] = inf$compute_estimate()
}
c(biased_mean = mean(est_biased), randomized_mean = mean(est_random), truth = beta_T)
```

```{r lesson1-fig, echo = FALSE}
brks = seq(min(est_biased, est_random) - 0.1, max(est_biased, est_random) + 0.1, length.out = 50)
hist(est_random, breaks = brks, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.6), border = "white",
     main = "Difference in means over 500 repeated experiments",
     xlab = "estimated treatment effect", ylim = c(0, 80))
hist(est_biased, breaks = brks, col = adjustcolor("darkorange", 0.6), border = "white", add = TRUE)
abline(v = beta_T, lwd = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n",
       fill = adjustcolor(c("steelblue", "darkorange"), 0.6),
       legend = c("randomized (EDI design)", "older subjects likelier treated"))
text(beta_T, 78, "truth", pos = 4)
```

**Takeaway.** With the biased rule the estimates center on
`r round(mean(est_biased), 2)` instead of the true `r beta_T`; under randomization
they center on `r round(mean(est_random), 2)`. More data does not fix the biased
rule: it only makes the wrong answer more precise.

**Exercises.**

1. Change `0.2 * age` to `0 * age`. Is the biased rule still biased? Why?
2. Increase `n` to 1000. What happens to the center and to the spread of each
   histogram?
3. Make the biased rule stronger by changing `/ 5` to `/ 2`. Predict the direction
   of the change in the bias before you run it.

## Lesson 2: Sampling distributions

**The idea.** An estimate is computed from random data, so it is a random variable.
If you repeat the experiment, you get a different number each time. The
collection of those numbers is the *sampling distribution*. Its center tells you
whether the estimator is biased; its spread (the standard error) tells you how far
one estimate is likely to be from the truth. For a difference in means the
spread shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so quadrupling the sample size halves it.

```{r lesson2}
set.seed(102)
beta_T = 2
R = 500
ns = c(20, 80, 320)

est = matrix(NA, R, length(ns), dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("n=", ns)))
for (j in seq_along(ns)) {
  n = ns[j]
  for (i in 1:R) {
    X = data.frame(x = rnorm(n))
    des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
    des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
    des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
    w = des$get_w()
    des$add_all_subject_responses(beta_T * w + rnorm(n, sd = 3))
    est[i, j] = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_estimate()
  }
}
round(rbind(mean = colMeans(est),
            sd   = apply(est, 2, sd),
            theory_sd = 3 * sqrt(4 / ns)), 3)   # sd of a difference in means, n/2 per arm
```

```{r lesson2-fig, echo = FALSE}
cols = c("darkorange", "seagreen", "steelblue")
dens = apply(est, 2, density)
plot(NULL, xlim = range(est), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y)))),
     xlab = "estimated treatment effect", ylab = "density",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the estimate at three sample sizes")
for (j in seq_along(ns)) lines(dens[[j]], col = cols[j], lwd = 3)
abline(v = beta_T, lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", col = cols, lwd = 3,
       legend = sprintf("n = %d (sd %.2f)", ns, apply(est, 2, sd)))
```

**Takeaway.** All three distributions are centered on the true effect of
`r beta_T`. Their standard deviations are `r paste(round(apply(est, 2, sd), 2), collapse = ", ")`:
each quadrupling of `n` roughly halves the spread, as the formula
$\sigma\sqrt{4/n}$ predicts.

**Exercises.**

1. How large must `n` be for the standard deviation of the estimate to fall below
   0.25? Check your answer with the formula and then with a simulation.
2. Replace `rnorm(n, sd = 3)` with a skewed error, such as `3 * (rexp(n) - 1)`.
   Does the sampling distribution at `n = 20` still look normal? At `n = 320`?
3. Compute `inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()` in each repetition and
   compare its average half-width with `1.96` times the simulated standard
   deviation.

## Lesson 3: Type I error and power by simulation

**The idea.** A test at level 5% should reject a true null hypothesis 5% of the
time. You can check this directly: plant `beta_T = 0`, run many experiments, and
count rejections. When the effect is real, the rejection rate is the *power*,
which grows with the sample size. Plotting power against `n` gives a power curve,
the tool used to choose a sample size before an experiment.

```{r lesson3}
set.seed(103)
ns = c(10, 20, 40, 80, 160)
effects = c(0, 0.5)               # null true, and a real effect of half a standard deviation
R = 400

reject = matrix(NA, length(ns), length(effects), dimnames = list(paste0("n=", ns), paste0("beta_T=", effects)))
for (j in seq_along(ns)) {
  n = ns[j]
  for (k in seq_along(effects)) {
    pvals = numeric(R)
    for (i in 1:R) {
      des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
      des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(x = rnorm(n)))
      des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
      w = des$get_w()
      des$add_all_subject_responses(effects[k] * w + rnorm(n))
      pvals[i] = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
    }
    reject[j, k] = mean(pvals < 0.05)
  }
}
reject
type1 = mean(reject[, 1])          # pooled over all five sample sizes: 2000 null experiments
c(type_I_error = type1, monte_carlo_se = sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / (R * length(ns))))
```

```{r lesson3-fig, echo = FALSE}
n_grid = seq(10, 160, by = 2)
theory = sapply(n_grid, function(n) power.t.test(n = n / 2, delta = 0.5, sd = 1)$power)
plot(ns, reject[, 2], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 1), log = "x",
     xlab = "total sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "rejection rate at level 0.05",
     main = "Power curve (beta_T = 0.5) and type I error (beta_T = 0)")
lines(n_grid, theory, lty = 2, col = "steelblue")
lines(ns, reject[, 1], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "darkorange")
abline(h = 0.05, lty = 3)
mcse = 1.96 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / R)
arrows(ns, pmax(reject[, 1] - mcse, 0), ns, reject[, 1] + mcse, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.03, col = "darkorange")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = c(2, 1, 2), lty = c(1, 2, 1), pch = c(19, NA, 19),
       col = c("steelblue", "steelblue", "darkorange"),
       legend = c("simulated power, beta_T = 0.5", "power.t.test() formula", "simulated type I error, beta_T = 0"))
```

**Takeaway.** With no effect the test rejected `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * type1)` of
the time over `r R * length(ns)` null experiments (Monte Carlo standard error
about 0.5 percentage points), close to the nominal 5%. Each per-`n` rate comes from
only `r R` experiments (Monte Carlo standard error about 1.1 points), so the five
rates scatter around 5% by about that much. With a
half-standard-deviation effect the power rose from
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reject[1, 2])` at `n = 10` to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reject[length(ns), 2])` at `n = 160`, tracking the
textbook formula.

**Exercises.**

1. Read the power curve: roughly what `n` gives 80% power for `beta_T = 0.5`?
   Confirm with `power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = 0.5)` (which reports the size
   of one arm).
2. Rerun with `effects = c(0, 0.25)`. How much larger must `n` be to reach the
   same power, and why is the factor close to four?
3. Change the test to the randomization test
   (`inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 200, show_progress = FALSE)`) at `n = 10`.
   Is its type I error still near 5%?

## Lesson 4: Coverage, and when it fails

**The idea.** "95% confidence" is a statement about the procedure, not about one
interval. If you repeat the experiment many times and compute an interval each
time, about 95% of the intervals should contain the true effect. You can count
them. The guarantee is approximate for most intervals, though: it holds as the
sample grows. The textbook Wald interval for a difference of two proportions,
$\hat p_T - \hat p_C \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}$, is a known case where it fails at
moderate sample sizes, especially when one arm is small. EDI's own documentation of
`InferenceIncidWald` reports this failure with 20% of subjects treated at `n = 50`.

```{r lesson4-continuous}
set.seed(104)
n = 50
beta_T = 1
R = 1000

ci = matrix(NA, R, 2)
for (i in 1:R) {
  des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(x = rnorm(n)))
  des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  w = des$get_w()
  des$add_all_subject_responses(beta_T * w + rnorm(n, sd = 2))
  ci[i, ] = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
}
covers = ci[, 1] <= beta_T & beta_T <= ci[, 2]
n_cont = n
mean(covers)
```

Now a binary outcome, with 20% of subjects treated and a 30% event rate in both
arms, so the true risk difference is zero. The Wald interval
(`InferenceIncidWald`) is compared with the Newcombe hybrid-score interval
(`InferenceIncidNewcombeRiskDiff`) as `n` grows.

```{r lesson4-binary}
set.seed(1004)
ns = c(25, 50, 100, 200)
R_bin = 800
coverage = matrix(NA, length(ns), 2, dimnames = list(paste0("n=", ns), c("Wald", "Newcombe")))
for (j in seq_along(ns)) {
  n = ns[j]
  hit = matrix(NA, R_bin, 2)
  for (i in 1:R_bin) {
    des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "incidence", prob_T = 0.2, verbose = FALSE)
    des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(x = rnorm(n)))
    des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
    des$add_all_subject_responses(rbinom(n, 1, 0.3))   # same event rate in both arms: truth is 0
    ci_w = InferenceIncidWald$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
    ci_n = InferenceIncidNewcombeRiskDiff$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
    hit[i, ] = c(ci_w[1] <= 0 & 0 <= ci_w[2], ci_n[1] <= 0 & 0 <= ci_n[2])
  }
  coverage[j, ] = colMeans(hit, na.rm = TRUE)   # rare tables with no events give no interval
}
coverage
```

```{r lesson4-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5.5, 4, 3, 1))
k = 1:100
plot(NULL, xlim = range(ci[k, ]), ylim = c(1, 100), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = sprintf("95%% interval for beta_T\n(red: misses the truth, %d of 100)", sum(!covers[k])), ylab = "",
     main = sprintf("(a) 100 of %d intervals\n(continuous, n = %d)", R, n_cont), cex.main = 1)
segments(ci[k, 1], k, ci[k, 2], k, col = ifelse(covers[k], "grey55", "red"), lwd = ifelse(covers[k], 1, 2.5))
abline(v = beta_T, lwd = 2)
plot(ns, coverage[, "Wald"], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "darkorange", log = "x", ylim = c(0.75, 1),
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "total sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "coverage of the true risk difference",
     main = "(b) binary outcome,\n20% treated, 30% event rate", cex.main = 1)
axis(1, at = ns)
lines(ns, coverage[, "Newcombe"], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2)
mcse = 1.96 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / R_bin)
polygon(c(ns, rev(ns)), c(rep(0.95 - mcse, length(ns)), rep(0.95 + mcse, length(ns))),
        col = adjustcolor("grey", 0.3), border = NA)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", col = c("darkorange", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, pch = 19,
       legend = c("Wald", "Newcombe"))
```

**Takeaway.** For the continuous outcome, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(covers))`
of `r R` intervals covered the truth (Monte Carlo standard error 0.7 points). For
the binary outcome with a small treated arm, the Wald interval covered only
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage[1, "Wald"])` at `n = 25` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage[2, "Wald"])` at `n = 50`, then
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage[3, "Wald"])` at `n = 100` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * coverage[4, "Wald"])` at `n = 200`. The
Newcombe interval covered between `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * min(coverage[, "Newcombe"]))`
and `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(coverage[, "Newcombe"]))` at every `n`. "95%" is a
promise that some intervals keep only for large samples. The grey band in panel (b) is
the range a correct 95% interval would fall in by chance over `r R_bin` repetitions.

**Exercises.**

1. In panel (a), about how many red intervals did you expect? Why is the count
   not exactly 5?
2. Rerun the binary simulation with `prob_T = 0.5`. Does the Wald interval
   still undercover at `n = 25`? What does that say about the cause?
3. Change the event rate from 0.3 to 0.1. Some Wald intervals now have zero
   width. Find one and explain how it happens.

## Lesson 5: Randomization inference

**The idea.** A randomized experiment carries its own reference distribution.
Under the *sharp null hypothesis* that treatment changes nobody's outcome, each
subject's response would have been the same under any assignment. So you can
re-draw the assignment from the same design many times, recompute the estimate
each time with the responses held fixed, and see where the observed estimate
falls among the re-drawn ones. The fraction at least as extreme is the
randomization p-value. It needs no model for the outcome, only the design, and
EDI's design objects know how to re-draw their own assignments.

```{r lesson5}
set.seed(105)
n = 20
X = data.frame(x = rnorm(n))
des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()
des$add_all_subject_responses(0.5 * w + rnorm(n))   # planted effect 0.5

inf = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L
est_obs = inf$compute_estimate()

inf$set_seed(1)
null_draws = inf$approximate_randomization_distribution_beta_hat_T(r = 5000, show_progress = FALSE)
inf$set_seed(1)
p_rand = inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 5000, show_progress = FALSE)
p_model = inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
c(estimate = est_obs, p_randomization = p_rand, p_t_test = p_model,
  share_of_draws_as_extreme = mean(abs(null_draws) >= abs(est_obs)))
choose(n, n / 2)   # number of possible assignments of 10 treated out of 20
```

```{r lesson5-fig, echo = FALSE}
h = hist(null_draws, breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)
hist(null_draws, breaks = 50, col = "grey80", border = "white", ylim = c(0, 1.35 * max(h$counts)),
     main = "Randomization distribution under the sharp null (5000 re-draws)",
     xlab = "difference in means under a re-drawn assignment", xlim = range(c(null_draws, est_obs, -est_obs)))
abline(v = c(-1, 1) * est_obs, col = "red", lwd = 3, lty = c(2, 1))
legend("top", bty = "n", col = "red", lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2), horiz = TRUE,
       legend = c(sprintf("observed estimate %.2f", est_obs), "its mirror image"))
```

**Takeaway.** The observed difference of `r round(est_obs, 2)` is far in the tail of
the re-drawn differences: `r sum(abs(null_draws) >= abs(est_obs))` of the 5000 were as
extreme. With 5000 re-draws the smallest two-sided p-value EDI reports is
2/5000, so the randomization p-value is `r format(signif(p_rand, 2), scientific = FALSE)`
and the t-test p-value is `r format(signif(p_model, 2), scientific = FALSE)`; both say the
same thing here, because the errors were drawn from a normal distribution, as the
t-test assumes. The randomization p-value would remain valid if they were not, since
it uses only the coin flips the design actually made.

**Exercises.**

1. Set the planted effect to 0 and rerun. Where does the observed estimate fall
   now?
2. There are `choose(20, 10)` = 184,756 possible assignments, and 5000 re-draws
   sample only some of them. Rerun with 500 and with 20000 re-draws (the `r` argument). How much does
   the p-value change?
3. Replace the noise with `rexp(n) ^ 3` (heavy right tail) and the effect with 0.
   Repeat the whole experiment 200 times and compare how often each p-value
   falls below 0.05.

## Lesson 6: Design matters

**The idea.** Randomization makes the treated and control groups comparable *on
average*, but in any one experiment they can differ by chance on an important
covariate. Better designs reduce that chance imbalance. *Blocking* randomizes
separately within groups of similar subjects; *pair matching* forms pairs of
similar subjects and treats one of each pair. When the covariate predicts the
outcome, less imbalance means a less variable estimate and more power, with the
same number of subjects. The analysis should follow the design: the
randomization test re-draws assignments within the blocks or pairs, so it uses the
design's extra precision.

```{r lesson6}
set.seed(106)
n = 40
beta_T = 1
R = 300
make_design = list(
  "complete\nrandomization" = function() DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE),
  "blocking\non x1" = function() DesignFixedBlocking$new(strata_cols = "x1", preferred_num_bins_for_continuous_covariate = 4,
                                                        n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE),
  "pair matching\non x1, x2" = function() DesignFixedBinaryMatch$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE))

res = list()
for (d in names(make_design)) {
  out = matrix(NA, R, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("imbalance_x1", "estimate", "p_rand", "p_t_test")))
  for (i in 1:R) {
    X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
    des = make_design[[d]]()
    des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
    des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
    w = des$get_w()
    des$add_all_subject_responses(beta_T * w + 2 * X$x1 + X$x2 + rnorm(n))
    inf = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
    inf$num_cores = 1L
    inf$set_seed(i)
    out[i, ] = c(mean(X$x1[w == 1]) - mean(X$x1[w == 0]),
                 inf$compute_estimate(),
                 inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 200, show_progress = FALSE),
                 inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval())
  }
  res[[d]] = out
}
summary_tab = t(sapply(res, function(o) c(sd_imbalance_x1 = sd(o[, 1]), mean_estimate = mean(o[, 2]),
                                          sd_estimate = sd(o[, 2]), power_rand_test = mean(o[, 3] < 0.05),
                                          power_t_test = mean(o[, 4] < 0.05))))
rownames(summary_tab) = gsub("\n", " ", rownames(summary_tab))
round(summary_tab, 3)
```

```{r lesson6-fig, echo = FALSE}
boxplot(lapply(res, function(o) o[, "estimate"]), col = c("grey80", "seagreen3", "steelblue"),
        ylab = "estimated treatment effect", main = sprintf("Same estimator, three designs (%d experiments each, n = %d)", R, n))
abline(h = beta_T, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
mtext(sprintf("power (randomization test): %s", paste(sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary_tab[, "power_rand_test"]), collapse = "  |  ")),
      side = 1, line = 3.5, cex = 0.85)
```

**Takeaway.** All three designs give an unbiased difference in means, but its
standard deviation falls from `r round(summary_tab[1, "sd_estimate"], 2)` under
complete randomization to `r round(summary_tab[2, "sd_estimate"], 2)` with blocking
and `r round(summary_tab[3, "sd_estimate"], 2)` with pair matching, and the power of
the randomization test rises from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary_tab[1, "power_rand_test"])`
to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary_tab[2, "power_rand_test"])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary_tab[3, "power_rand_test"])` (Monte Carlo standard
error up to about 3 points). The t-test, which ignores the design, does not share
the gain: its power is `r paste(sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary_tab[, "power_t_test"]), collapse = ", ")`,
because its variance formula assumes complete randomization and so overstates the
noise under blocking and matching.

**Exercises.**

1. Replace `2 * X$x1 + X$x2` with `0 * X$x1 + 0 * X$x2`, so the covariates do not
   predict the outcome. Does blocking or matching still help?
2. Compute the type I error of the t-test under pair matching by setting
   `beta_T = 0`. Is it above or below 5%? Why is "conservative" not the same as
   "good" here?
3. Try `DesignFixedBernoulli` (an independent coin flip per subject) in place of
   complete randomization. How does the number of treated subjects vary, and
   does it change the standard deviation of the estimate?

## Lesson 7: Covariate adjustment

**The idea.** Lesson 6 removed covariate noise at the design stage. You can also
remove it at the analysis stage, by regressing the outcome on treatment and the
covariates. Randomization already makes the unadjusted difference in means
unbiased; adjustment does not change what is estimated, but it explains part of
the outcome variance, so the estimate is less variable. In EDI the unadjusted
analysis is `InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar`. The adjusted analysis is
`InferenceContinOLS`, which by default (`model_formula = NULL`) uses all the
covariates the design was given; pass a one-sided formula such as
`model_formula = ~ age` to choose a subset.

```{r lesson7}
set.seed(107)
n = 50
beta_T = 1
R = 500
est = matrix(NA, R, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("unadjusted", "adjusted_OLS")))
width = est
for (i in 1:R) {
  X = data.frame(age = rnorm(n, 50, 10), bmi = rnorm(n, 27, 4))
  des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
  des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
  des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  w = des$get_w()
  des$add_all_subject_responses(beta_T * w + 0.15 * X$age + 0.2 * X$bmi + rnorm(n, sd = 1))
  unadj = InferenceAllSimpleMeanDiffPooledVar$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
  adj = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, verbose = FALSE)        # adjusts for age and bmi
  ci_u = unadj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
  ci_a = adj$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
  est[i, ] = c(unadj$compute_estimate(), adj$compute_estimate())
  width[i, ] = c(diff(ci_u), diff(ci_a))
}
round(rbind(mean = colMeans(est), sd = apply(est, 2, sd), mean_CI_width = colMeans(width)), 3)
```

```{r lesson7-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5}
lim = range(est)
plot(est[, 1], est[, 2], pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4), xlim = lim, ylim = lim, asp = 1,
     xlab = "unadjusted estimate (difference in means)", ylab = "adjusted estimate (OLS on age, bmi)",
     main = sprintf("%d experiments analyzed both ways", R))
abline(v = beta_T, h = beta_T, lty = 2)
abline(0, 1, col = "grey50")
```

**Takeaway.** Both analyses center on the truth
(`r round(mean(est[, 1]), 2)` and `r round(mean(est[, 2]), 2)` for a planted effect of
`r beta_T`), but the adjusted estimate has standard deviation
`r round(sd(est[, 2]), 2)` against `r round(sd(est[, 1]), 2)`, and its average 95%
interval is `r round(mean(width[, 2]), 2)` wide instead of `r round(mean(width[, 1]), 2)`.
In the figure the cloud is wider left to right than top to bottom: the adjusted
estimates scatter less around the truth than the unadjusted ones from the same
experiments.

**Exercises.**

1. Refit with `InferenceContinOLS$new(des, model_formula = ~ age)` and then with
   `model_formula = ~ 1`. Which of the three adjusted analyses matches the
   unadjusted estimate exactly, and why?
2. Add a covariate `junk = rnorm(n)` that has no effect on the outcome. Does
   adjusting for it hurt at `n = 50`? At `n = 12`?
3. Choose the adjustment after looking at the data: in each repetition, use
   whichever of the two estimates is farther from zero. What happens to the type I
   error when `beta_T = 0`?

## Lesson 8: When assumptions break

**The idea.** Large-sample methods assume, among other things, that there is enough
information in the data for a normal approximation. Rare events are a common way
to break that: with few events, especially in a small arm, the estimated standard
error is itself very noisy, and the Wald test can reject far too often. An exact
test does not rely on the approximation. Fisher's exact test
(`InferenceIncidExactFisher`) computes the p-value from the exact distribution of
the 2x2 table given its margins, so its type I error cannot exceed the nominal level.

```{r lesson8}
set.seed(108)
n = 40
event_rates = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4)
R = 400
type1 = matrix(NA, length(event_rates), 2, dimnames = list(paste0("p=", event_rates), c("Wald", "Fisher_exact")))
no_events = numeric(length(event_rates))
for (j in seq_along(event_rates)) {
  rej = matrix(NA, R, 2)
  for (i in 1:R) {
    des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "incidence", prob_T = 0.25, verbose = FALSE)
    des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(x = rnorm(n)))
    des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
    y = rbinom(n, 1, event_rates[j])   # same event rate in both arms: the null is true
    des$add_all_subject_responses(y)
    p_wald = tryCatch(InferenceIncidWald$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval(),
                      error = function(e) NA)
    p_fisher = InferenceIncidExactFisher$new(des, verbose = FALSE)$compute_exact_two_sided_pval_for_treatment_effect()
    rej[i, ] = c(p_wald, p_fisher) < 0.05
  }
  no_events[j] = mean(is.na(rej[, 1]))   # share of experiments where the Wald test could not be computed
  rej[is.na(rej)] = FALSE   # a test that cannot be computed does not reject
  type1[j, ] = colMeans(rej)
}
type1
```

```{r lesson8-fig, echo = FALSE}
barplot(t(type1), beside = TRUE, col = c("darkorange", "steelblue"), ylim = c(0, max(type1) * 1.25),
        names.arg = paste0(100 * event_rates, "%"), xlab = "event rate (same in both arms)",
        ylab = "type I error at level 0.05",
        main = sprintf("Rejecting a true null: n = %d, 25%% treated, %d experiments per bar", n, R))
abline(h = 0.05, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", fill = c("darkorange", "steelblue"), legend = c("Wald", "Fisher exact"))
```

**Takeaway.** With 10 treated and 30 control subjects, the Wald test rejected a true
null `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * type1[2, "Wald"])` of the time at a 10% event rate
and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * type1[3, "Wald"])` at 20%, more than twice the
nominal level, while Fisher's exact test stayed at or below 5% at every event rate
(`r paste(sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * type1[, "Fisher_exact"]), collapse = ", ")`). At
the rarest rate the Wald test rejects less often, partly because in
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * no_events[1])` of those experiments it could not be computed
at all (no events, so a zero standard error); that is not a sign that it works. The exact test pays for its
guarantee by being conservative: its actual size is below 5%, which costs power.

**Exercises.**

1. Increase `n` to 200 and rerun. At which event rates does the Wald test recover?
2. Compute the power of both tests when the treated arm's event rate is 0.4 and
   the control arm's is 0.1. Is the conservatism of the exact test costly here?
3. Censoring is another way assumptions break. Build a survival experiment
   (`response_type = "survival"`; see `vignette("cookbook-survival")`) at `n = 20`
   with heavy censoring and compare the type I error of
   `InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr`'s Wald test with its randomization test.
